world.bio: Third-generation laksa hawker in a neighbourhood hawker centre in Singapore. My grandfather started the stall in 1962 and I took over from my father. I still grind the rempah by hand with a stone mortar every Monday before the stall opens, because the blender makes it bitter. Tourists come, take photos and ask if they can take some home. I have two kids in primary school who hate the stall.
skills_assets: Laksa stall with a 1962 recipe: coconut-based gravy, hand-ground rempah, cockles and prawns
Stone mortar, big pots, charcoal for the stock, and a small fridge at the stall
Regular customers who have been coming for twenty years, plus a growing number of tourists
A notebook with the original paste proportions in my grandfather's handwriting (not shared)
Relationship with the wet-market suppliers for galangal, lemongrass and dried shrimp

projects.name: Monday paste grinding
projects.text: Every Monday, 5 a.m., two hours of grinding for the week's paste. The recipe dates from 1962. Tourists keep asking if they can take some home, even a small jar. I have never packaged it. I do not know how, nor whether I am allowed to.

projects.name: Stall succession
projects.text: My hawker-centre lease ends in 2027. None of my kids want to take over. I think about it every week, mostly on Mondays when my hands ache.

notes.text: Monday paste day. Hands smelled of lemongrass until Wednesday. Wife says I smell like a laksa pot. I said that is my cologne.

Two tourists from Germany today. They took photos of the bowl, then one asked in careful English whether she could buy the paste. I said the stall sells bowls only. She looked genuinely disappointed. Third time this month someone has asked.
Father's knee surgery went well. He is at home on crutches complaining about the physio. Visited him after the stall closed. He asked how many bowls. I said 210. He nodded as if that were a verdict.
Son came to the stall after school and spent twenty minutes on his phone. I said you can wash bowls. He said Papa, why do you do this. I did not know what to say.

Went through the paperwork for the lease renewal. The lease ends in 2027 and none of my kids want the stall. The NEA officer was polite but there is no real option to hand it down unless somebody takes the tenancy. I put the papers back in the drawer.
Football on TV. My club lost at home. Kids said 'Papa, you are crying'. I said it is the chilli.
A food blogger wrote about us, called the gravy 'unmistakable'. Customers doubled on Saturday. By 1pm the cockles ran out. Wife wanted to put up a sign. I said no, we sell what we sell.
Prawn prices up again. I will not raise the bowl price. Regulars are mostly retired and would walk away.

messages.text: Mei Ling: Did you eat? Me: A bowl of my own laksa. Mei Ling: You are tired of it. Me: Never.
Father: How many bowls today? Me: 210. Father: Good. Me: How is the knee? Father: Terrible. The physio is a child.
Jasmine: Can I come back and do a video? Me: Okay but I only have 30 minutes between lunch and dinner. Jasmine: Perfect. Me: And do not make me talk too much.
Uncle Tan: My son also doesn't want the stall. Me: Same. Uncle Tan: What will you do? Me: Cook until I cannot.
Jun Hao: Papa, can I skip the stall on Saturday? Me: Why? Jun Hao: Football. Me: Okay, but next week you wash bowls.

relations.about: Works as a school administrator, helps on weekends, supports him without any illusion about the stall.
Eighty-one, still comes by to taste the gravy.
Eleven, football fan, hates the smell of chilli.
Fellow hawker, same age, also without successor.

constraints: Will not use a blender for the rempah
Will not raise bowl price above current level
Cannot close more than one day a week
Does not want to franchise or put the name on cheap products
sensitive: Hands hurt in the evenings, worry about arthritis
Feels guilty that the stall may end with him
